# Zelta Design

> Zelta Design is a full-service architecture firm in Nutley, New Jersey, specializing in restaurant and commercial projects. The firm has completed over 2,500 projects for +40 brands and works nationwide, licensed in 25 states and adding states as clients need them. It handles a project end to end: site survey, schematic design, construction documents, permitting and plan review, code and accessibility compliance, MEP coordination and construction administration.

## Key facts

- Legal name: Zelta Design
- Headquarters: 139 Chestnut Street, Nutley, NJ 07110
- Phone: 973-933-6636
- Email: hello@zeltadesign.com
- Principal Architect: Erik Liepins, RA (Owner)
- Licensed jurisdictions today (25): Arkansas, Connecticut, Washington, D.C., Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, North Carolina, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, Vermont, Wisconsin, West Virginia
- Service area: the United States outside California, Alaska and Hawaii. The firm gets licensed in a new state when a client brings a project there, before any drawing needs a seal.
- Completed projects: over 2,500
- Brands served: +40
- Projects published on this site: 145 (99 with photography)
- Sector focus: quick-service restaurants, fast casual, cafes, and commercial tenant fit-outs

- [Capabilities](https://www.zeltadesign.com/services/): services, process, and project enquiries.
- [Resources](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/): guides to restaurant permits, approvals, design and timelines.
- [Permits by State](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/topic/permits-by-state/): Start with the guide for your location. These guides explain how zoning, building permits, health review and inspections fit together. The city or county handling your project determines the local process, even when the state sets the code.
- [Permitting](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/topic/permitting/): Understand the approval process before you set an opening date. Start with the timeline, then work through health review, fire protection and other approvals that apply to your restaurant. The final guides cover review comments and the sign-offs needed to open.
- [Franchise](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/topic/franchise/): A brand prototype is the starting point for a location, but the site still needs its own design and approvals. Begin with brand review, then read about coordinating multiple locations or the guide for your brand.
- [Design](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/topic/design/): See how the building, kitchen and customer experience shape a restaurant layout. Start with kitchen systems and accessibility, then explore the formats and equipment that apply to your site. Construction documents bring those decisions together for pricing, permitting and building.
- [Planning](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/topic/planning/): Check whether a site can support your restaurant before committing to the lease or construction. Start with feasibility and the lease checklist, then learn how to choose your project team, define the scope and prepare the information they need.
- [Glossary](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/glossary/): plain-English restaurant design and permitting terms.
- [About](https://www.zeltadesign.com/about/): the firm, the team and how projects run.
- [Contact](https://www.zeltadesign.com/contact/): start a project.

## Guides

- [Restaurant Architect, Engineer, Expediter or Contractor?](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/architect-engineer-expediter-contractor/): On a restaurant project the architect designs the space and leads the sealed permit drawings, engineers usually design and seal the building systems, a civil engineer handles site work, an expediter files and tracks permits, and the contractor builds and in many places pulls the permits. Who seals which sheet depends on the state and the scope, and who coordinates whom depends on what each contract says, so assign both in writing before work starts.
- [Opening a Restaurant in Connecticut: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/connecticut-restaurant-permits/): Connecticut has no county government, so a restaurant's zoning, building permit and fire marshal review all come from the town, under one statewide building code and fire safety code. The kitchen goes to the town health department or a regional health district that may sit in another town. On tribal land, the tribal nation's own agencies take the place of the town, and other approvals depend on the site and scope.
- [What Your Restaurant Architect Does During Construction](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/construction-administration/): During construction the architect can answer the contractor's questions, review shop drawings and product submittals, handle changes that affect the approved permit drawings and support inspections through closeout. How much of that is included depends on the architect's contract: some proposals include it, others bill it as additional services. The contractor, not the architect, runs the job site.
- [Do I Need an Architect to Open a Restaurant?](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/do-i-need-an-architect-for-a-restaurant/): For a new restaurant, or a fit-out that changes the layout, kitchen or exits, usually yes: the building department will want drawings sealed by a design professional licensed in that state, and in New Jersey the building design must come from an architect. Exemptions exist, but most cover small, low-cost work or buildings that are not used for gatherings, and the local building official decides whether yours qualifies.
- [Restaurant Drive-Thru Design and Stacking Requirements](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/drive-thru-design/): A drive-thru is designed from the lot inward: how many cars the lane holds, whether there is an order point or only a pickup window, how cars enter and leave, and which way the building faces. The local zoning code usually sets the minimum stacking, the brand adds its own standards, and the town reviews the lane as a site change, so the building plan follows the lane.
- [As-Built Drawings and Site Surveys for Restaurants](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/existing-conditions-survey/): Restaurant drawings can only be as accurate as what is known about the space. An existing conditions survey measures and records the real dimensions, structure and building systems before design starts, so the layout, equipment and permit set rest on verified facts rather than on a prototype or an old landlord drawing. What the survey cannot see is recorded as unknown, not assumed.
- [Opening a Restaurant in Florida: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/florida-restaurant-permits/): In Florida, the building permit comes from the city building department, or from the county for unincorporated land, under the statewide Florida Building Code. The local fire official reviews fire and life safety. Food licensing is state run: most restaurants are licensed by DBPR's Division of Hotels and Restaurants, while bakeries, grocery and convenience stores fall under FDACS. Zoning, grease, signs and other approvals depend on the site and scope.
- [How Franchise Brand Design Approvals Work](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/franchise-brand-approvals/): Before a franchise location is built, the brand usually reviews its design in stages: a layout or test fit, then a design development set, then a formal release. The exact steps differ by brand. Brand approval is separate from the city permit; a location needs both, and a change after either approval usually has to go back through review.
- [Building a Restaurant from the Ground Up on a Pad Site](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/ground-up-restaurant-pad-site/): A ground-up restaurant on a pad site runs as a site project and a building project that overlap. The survey and soils report come first, a civil engineer leads the site plan, and the architect adapts the brand prototype to the lot. Building drawings can progress during land use review, but in most towns the building permit is not issued until the land use approval and its conditions are met.
- [Health Department Plan Review for Restaurants](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/health-department-plan-review/): Before a restaurant is built, converted or substantially remodeled, the health authority usually reviews its food service plans: layout, equipment, sinks, finishes, menu and food safety procedures. Who reviews them varies by state, county, town and, on tribal land, tribal nation, and the packet needs as much from the operator as from the architect, so start it alongside the building drawings.
- [How to Choose a Restaurant Architect: Questions to Ask](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/how-to-choose-a-restaurant-architect/): Choose a restaurant architect who holds an active license in your state, has designed your format and ideally your brand, is clear about who provides and coordinates the engineering, starts from a real survey, has a plan for permits and plan review comments, and defines construction support in writing. Then compare proposals scope for scope, because two fees only compare fairly when they cover the same work.
- [Landlord Work vs Tenant Work: Shell Types and the Work Letter](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/landlord-vs-tenant-work/): Landlord work is whatever the lease makes the landlord responsible for; tenant work is everything the lease leaves to you, even when the two happen at the same time. Shell labels like cold shell, vanilla shell and white box have no fixed definition, so the work letter decides who provides the electrical service, gas, heating and cooling, restrooms and grease interceptor. Each item needs a provider, a size and a connection point written down.
- [Opening a Restaurant in a Mall or Transit Hub: Landlord Rules](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/mall-and-transit-restaurants/): In a mall, outlet center or transit hub, the property owner's criteria sit on top of the building code. They can decide your equipment, rooftop units, signs, labor and the order of reviews. Many leases require landlord approval of drawings before you file for permits, so confirm the sequence from the lease and the reviewing authority before design starts.
- [Opening a Restaurant in Maryland: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/maryland-restaurant-permits/): In Maryland, a restaurant's building permit comes from the county or, inside some cities, from the city, under building codes the state requires every jurisdiction to use. The local health department must approve kitchen plans before construction, fire review sits with the state or a county fire office depending on the address, and in Prince George's County the regional planning commission checks zoning before a use and occupancy permit is issued.
- [Opening Many Restaurant Locations with One Architect](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/multi-unit-restaurant-rollout/): A multi-unit rollout goes faster with one architect because the brand prototype, drawing standards and permit tracking stay the same from store to store, while each site still gets its own survey, code review and permit path. The prototype is the starting point; every location is still its own building, landlord and jurisdiction.
- [Opening a Restaurant in New Jersey: Zoning, Boards and Permits](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/new-jersey-restaurant-permits/): In New Jersey, a restaurant deals with two separate systems: the town's land use approvals, from a zoning permit up to a planning board or zoning board hearing, and a construction permit under the statewide Uniform Construction Code. Land use approvals come first because the construction office checks them before releasing the permit. The local health authority approves the kitchen plans on its own track, and the construction official issues the certificate of occupancy after final inspections.
- [Opening a Restaurant in New York Outside NYC: Permits](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/new-york-restaurant-permits-outside-nyc/): Outside New York City, a restaurant's building permit usually comes from the city, town or village where the property sits, under the statewide Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code, though a few local governments have handed enforcement to their county or the state. The same local government runs zoning, which can mean a special use permit or site plan approval, and the county or state health office issues the food service permit. The first job is working out which local government you are actually in.
- [Opening a Restaurant in North Carolina: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/north-carolina-restaurant-permits/): In North Carolina, the city or county inspections department reviews the building under the statewide North Carolina State Building Code, and fire safety is reviewed locally. Kitchen plans go to the state's Plan Review Unit if the restaurant is a chain or franchise with ten or more locations, and to the county health department if it is independent. Zoning and other approvals depend on the site and the scope of work.
- [Opening a Restaurant in NYC: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/nyc-restaurant-permits/): In New York City, the Department of Buildings approves the construction drawings and issues the work permit, filed online by a New York licensed architect or engineer with the owner's authorization. Other agencies join depending on the building and the scope: asbestos clearance before the permit, Landmarks review in designated buildings, fire department requirements, separate sign permits and the Health Department permit to operate. Approval of the drawings, the work permit and permission to serve food are three different steps.
- [Opening a Restaurant in Ohio: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/ohio-restaurant-permits/): In Ohio, the building permit comes from a city, county or township building department certified by the state, or from the state's Division of Industrial Compliance where no certified department covers commercial work. The local health district must approve the kitchen layout and equipment in writing before that work is built, and zoning and design boards are local. Finding out who covers your address is the first job.
- [Opening a Dave's Hot Chicken: Design, Permits and Build-Out](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/opening-a-daves-hot-chicken/): A Dave's Hot Chicken is a frying kitchen wrapped in a bold, mural-heavy interior, and it opens in city storefronts, strip centers and freestanding drive-thru buildings. Many of the stores we design are conversions of former retail space, so the hood, make-up air, grease control and change of use decide the schedule as much as the design does.
- [Opening a Dunkin': Design, Permits and Build-Out](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/opening-a-dunkin/): A new Dunkin' is shaped by its format, from a freestanding drive-thru to a walk-up city counter or a shop shared with Baskin-Robbins, and by the version of the brand's design and equipment package approved for that store. The equipment drives the power, plumbing and drains, so settle it before the permit drawings, and expect the brand, landlord and town each to review their part.
- [Opening a Popeyes: Design, Permits and Build-Out](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/opening-a-popeyes/): A new Popeyes is shaped by two things: its format, which ranges from a freestanding drive-thru to a multi-level city store or a food court counter, and its frying kitchen, which drives the hood, make-up air, grease and fire suppression design. Settle both early, because they decide which approvals the store needs and how long the engineering takes.
- [Opening or Remodeling a Taco Bell: Design, Permits and Build-Out](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/opening-a-taco-bell/): A Taco Bell needs two approvals that run side by side: the brand's design review, which ends in its Notice to Proceed, and the local permits for the building, site and signs. The format you choose, from a freestanding drive-thru to a city storefront or a two-level Cantina, decides which reviews apply, so settle it before design starts.
- [Opening a Restaurant in Pennsylvania: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/pennsylvania-restaurant-permits/): In Pennsylvania, the building code is a statewide baseline, the Uniform Construction Code, but who enforces it is chosen parcel by parcel: the municipality's own staff, a private agency it hires, a shared regional office or the state Department of Labor and Industry, which also has sole jurisdiction over state-owned buildings. Zoning comes from the municipality, the food license from the state Department of Agriculture or a county or local health department, and grease approval often from the sewer authority. Identifying the right reviewers for the exact parcel is the first job.
- [Restaurant Pickup Design: Mobile Orders, Drivers and Kiosks](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/pickup-and-delivery-design/): A quick-service restaurant now serves several kinds of customer at once: people ordering at the counter or a kiosk, app customers collecting a bag, delivery drivers, and sometimes a drive-thru or walk-up window. Good design aims to give each group its own spot, so pickup traffic stays out of the ordering line as much as the room allows. The pickup shelf, the kiosks and the driver hand-off belong in the first test fit, not added at the end.
- [Permit Comments or Rejection? How to Respond and Get Approved](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/plan-review-comments/): Plan review comments are the reviewer's list of what must change or be explained before a permit can be issued. They are not a denial. Answer every comment by number in a response letter that says exactly what changed and where, send a revised sealed set that agrees with itself, and include the owner items the reviewer asked for. A complete response gives the reviewer what is needed to close each comment, though only the reviewer decides when the file is approved.
- [Restaurant ADA Requirements: Entrances, Seating and Restrooms](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-accessibility-ada/): A restaurant has to meet two accessibility rulebooks: the federal Americans with Disabilities Act and the accessibility chapter of the building code your state adopted. The entrance, the counters, the dining surfaces, the restrooms and the route from parking are where most requirements land. In an existing space, an alteration brings its own upgrade duties, and the federal duty to remove barriers where that is readily achievable applies whether or not you renovate.
- [How Much Does a Restaurant Architect Cost?](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-architect-cost/): A restaurant architect's fee depends mostly on project type and scope. In our own proposals across 324 projects, a remodel of an existing restaurant ran about three quarters of an inline fit-out, a ground-up drive-thru about one and a third times and a multi-level urban restaurant about 1.7 times. One RSMeans model for a new 5,000-square-foot restaurant uses a 7 percent architectural-fee allowance based on 2019 national data; it is not a current quote or a fit-out benchmark.
- [What's in a Restaurant Architect's Proposal (and What Isn't)](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-architect-proposal/): A restaurant architect's proposal should say what will be delivered in each phase, from the site survey to sealed permit drawings, which engineering is included, what the schedule depends on, how the fee is paid and what is excluded. Exclusions and assumptions matter as much as the scope: they show which other consultants your site may need and which events would change the fee.
- [Restaurant Sites: Pad, Inline, End-Cap or Food Court?](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-building-types/): The site type decides who reviews your restaurant before the building department and how much you control. A freestanding pad brings zoning and site plan review but full control of the lot. An inline or end-cap unit depends on the landlord and the shell. A food court or transit unit adds the property owner's own design review and shared systems.
- [How Do You Get a Certificate of Occupancy for a Restaurant?](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-certificate-of-occupancy/): A certificate of occupancy is the building department's approval that a finished space may be occupied for its approved use. Which inspections and sign-offs it depends on varies by jurisdiction, but it usually follows the trade finals and any fire or zoning sign-offs the office requires. It is separate from the health department's permit to operate and from a business license, so a restaurant typically needs both building closeout and permission to operate before it opens.
- [Restaurant Permit Drawings: What's in the Set](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-construction-documents/): A restaurant construction document set is the sealed package of drawings a building department reviews and a contractor builds from. It covers the architecture plus the engineering the space needs, and every sheet has to agree with every other sheet. Some parts, often sprinkler and fire alarm drawings, may be prepared by specialty contractors and filed separately, so the set should say exactly who provides what.
- [Does a Restaurant Need Sprinklers? Fire Protection Explained](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-fire-protection/): Whether a restaurant needs sprinklers or a fire alarm depends on the code your state adopted, the size of the fire area, the occupant load, the floor it sits on and the building around it, not on the brand. Cooking that produces grease or smoke generally needs a grease-rated hood with its own fire suppression system. Fire review is often a separate filing with its own reviewer and inspections, and it can hold up the certificate of occupancy after the building permit is issued.
- [Restaurant Hood, Grease Trap and Gas Requirements](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-kitchen-mep/): Three systems drive the engineering in a restaurant kitchen: the exhaust hood with its fire suppression and make-up air, the grease interceptor that keeps fats out of the sewer, and the gas and electric service that feeds the equipment. Each depends on the building, the landlord and the local sewer authority or utility as well as the drawings, so each needs answers before the layout is final.
- [Restaurant Lease Checklist: What Your Architect Should Check](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-lease-checklist/): Before you sign a restaurant lease, have an architect confirm and record the building facts the lease depends on: the zoning use, utility sizes, a route for kitchen exhaust, grease, the roof, restrooms and sign rights. Your attorney drafts and negotiates the lease; the architect hands the attorney the list of facts that need to be written in and who is responsible for each.
- [Restaurant Owner Checklist: What Your Architect Needs and When](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-owner-checklist/): The architect controls the drawings, but the schedule also depends on what the owner side supplies: the lease and landlord drawings at the start, layout and equipment decisions during design, and signatures, the legal entity, contractor details, construction value, menu and landlord authorization at permit time. Having each item ready before the stage that needs it removes avoidable waits; it cannot shorten an agency's own review.
- [Restaurant Build-Out Timeline: From Lease to Opening](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-permit-timeline/): A restaurant build-out moves through nine linked stages: feasibility, survey, design, brand and landlord review, permits, ordering long-lead equipment, construction, final inspections and the certificate of occupancy, then opening. The total length depends on which approvals your site needs, which must come first, how fast decisions are made and how long each agency takes, so a realistic schedule is built from those gates rather than from a single number.
- [Restaurant Permits and Licenses Checklist: Every Approval](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-permits-and-licenses-checklist/): Opening a restaurant takes two sets of approvals. The building side covers zoning, any board approval, the building permit, health plan review, fire review, signs and the certificate of occupancy; the business side covers your tax registrations, business license, food manager certificate and any liquor license. Which office issues each one varies by address, so build the list for your site before you sign the lease.
- [Remodeling a Restaurant: What Triggers Code Upgrades](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-remodels/): A restaurant remodel is reviewed by what it changes. Like-for-like replacement and finishes may need little or no permit, while reconfigured space, new systems and new equipment usually need drawings, and exterior or site changes can bring in zoning. Altering customer areas also brings federal accessibility duties for the path to them, up to a cost limit, so define the scope item by item before design.
- [Restaurant Sign Permits: Zoning, Landlords and Historic Review](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-signage-permits/): A restaurant sign usually needs several separate approvals: the brand's sign standard, the landlord under the lease's sign criteria, the town under its zoning sign code and sign permit, and in a historic district, a preservation commission. Sign codes vary widely from town to town, so the allowed signage should be checked before the lease is signed and the design is fixed.
- [Will This Site Work? Restaurant Feasibility Before You Sign](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-site-feasibility/): A feasibility study answers one question before you commit money: can this site legally and physically hold your restaurant, and what would it take? It combines a test fit of your brand's layout, a zoning and code check, and a look at utilities, exhaust, grease and the roof. The result lists the risks, the investigations still needed and the likely upgrades, each marked confirmed or still open.
- [Putting a Restaurant in a Historic Building](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurants-in-historic-buildings/): In a locally designated historic district or landmark, a preservation commission usually has to approve the exterior changes a restaurant needs, and in many cities that approval must come before the building permit is issued. The hard parts are usually the sign, the kitchen exhaust and the storefront, so design those with the commission's rules in mind from the first sketch, and have your attorney protect you in the lease.
- [Adding Rooftop Units to a Restaurant: Curbs, Dunnage, Structure](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/rooftop-units-structural/): A restaurant adds weight and holes to a roof: heating and cooling units, a kitchen exhaust fan, make-up air and often walk-in condensers. Before any of it is set, someone has to confirm the roof framing can carry the load where the equipment sits, decide whether each unit goes on a curb or on raised steel dunnage, and follow the landlord's roof rules. Where the framing is hidden, plan a field check once demolition exposes it, and get any added support designed and accepted before the units are set.
- [Turning a Retail Space into a Restaurant: Change of Use](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/second-generation-restaurant-space/): Turning a store, bank or office into a restaurant raises two separate questions. Zoning asks whether a restaurant is a permitted use, needs a special or conditional approval, or is prohibited, which may require rezoning, a use variance where legally available, or a different site. The building code asks whether the new use is a change of occupancy that brings stricter requirements. A former restaurant can skip some of this, but only if the use has not lapsed and the kitchen systems suit your menu.
- [Kiosks, Counters and Pickup-Only Stores: Designing Small](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/small-footprint-restaurants/): A small restaurant works when every square foot has one job. The big decisions are whether to offer seats at all, how the brand's equipment and storage fit behind a short counter, and how customers and staff move through a tight plan with an accessible route intact. Small does not exempt a store from the health code, accessibility rules or the building code, although some code provisions do scale with size and occupant load.
- [Opening a Restaurant in South Carolina: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/south-carolina-restaurant-permits/): In South Carolina, the building permit comes from the city if the site is inside city limits and from the county if not, under building codes adopted statewide. The food permit comes from the South Carolina Department of Agriculture, which took over retail food safety in 2024. The local business license usually follows the certificate of occupancy, and other approvals depend on the site and scope.
- [Can You Speed Up a Restaurant Permit? What Actually Works](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/speeding-up-restaurant-permits/): Sometimes, but only one review at a time. Some cities sell an expedited building plan review, New York City lets the architect professionally certify qualifying filings, and Florida lets an owner hire a private provider for plan review and inspections. Each can move its own review sooner, while every other required approval still controls when the permit issues. Filing a complete package once, in the right order, is the habit that helps every review.
- [Opening a Restaurant in Tennessee: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/tennessee-restaurant-permits/): In Tennessee, building plans for a restaurant are reviewed by the local code office if the State Fire Marshal's Office has approved that city or county as an exempt jurisdiction, and otherwise by the state when the building meets its submittal triggers. The state enforces its adopted codes where it has jurisdiction; exempt local governments enforce their own qualifying adopted editions. Kitchen plans go to the Tennessee Department of Health or, in Davidson, Hamilton, Knox, Madison and Shelby counties, the county health department. Grease programs and contractor licensing add their own steps depending on the city and the scope.
- [Getting Kitchen Exhaust Out of a City Storefront](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/urban-restaurant-exhaust/): In a city storefront with other floors above, a kitchen that needs a grease hood also needs a legal path for its exhaust: up through a shaft to the roof, up the outside of the rear wall, or out through a facade louver where the code and the reviewing agencies allow it. Which path works depends on the building, the landlord and, in historic districts, the preservation reviewers. Confirm it before you sign the lease, because without one the site cannot run a menu that needs a hood.
- [Opening a Restaurant in Virginia: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/virginia-restaurant-permits/): In Virginia, the building department of the county, city or town that covers the parcel issues the building permit under the statewide Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. The local health department reviews the kitchen plans under state food rules, and a local fire marshal's office usually reviews sprinkler and hood suppression plans. The code is the same everywhere, but each locality runs its own process, and other approvals depend on the scope of the work.
- [Opening a Restaurant in West Virginia: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/west-virginia-restaurant-permits/): In West Virginia, a restaurant usually deals with three separate reviewers: the county or town that enforces the State Building Code, the State Fire Marshal's plan review, and the local health department. Where a county or town has zoning, it often has to clear before the building permit issues. Which offices apply depends on the parcel and the scope, so confirm them first.

- [Taco Bell in New Jersey](https://www.zeltadesign.com/brands/taco-bell/new-jersey/): 15 locations.
